shared.title: How Desert Plants Save Water
shared.text:
Plants that live in deserts face a constant problem: they need carbon dioxide from the air to make food, but opening the small pores on their leaves to take in that gas also lets precious water escape. Many desert plants have solved this problem with a special form of photosynthesis called CAM.

Most plants open their pores, called stomata, during the day, when sunlight powers photosynthesis. CAM plants, such as cacti and pineapples, reverse this schedule. They open their stomata at night, when temperatures are cooler and the air is more humid, so far less water evaporates. During the night, the plants store carbon dioxide in the form of an acid. When the sun rises, they close their stomata tightly and release the stored carbon dioxide inside their own tissues, using it to carry out photosynthesis.

This strategy is remarkably efficient. Some CAM plants lose only a fraction of the water that ordinary plants lose while producing the same amount of food. However, the approach has a cost: because a plant can store only a limited amount of carbon dioxide overnight, CAM plants usually grow slowly. In harsh, dry environments, though, surviving matters more than growing quickly.

shared.title: Why we remember unfinished tasks
shared.text:
Today I want to talk about something you've probably experienced. Have you ever noticed that you keep thinking about a task you didn't finish, but once it's done, it disappears from your mind? In the 1920s, a psychologist named Bluma Zeigarnik became curious about this. The story goes that she noticed waiters in a restaurant could remember complicated orders perfectly, but only until the orders were paid for. After that, the details seemed to vanish.

So Zeigarnik designed an experiment. She gave people a series of simple tasks, like solving puzzles, and she interrupted some of the tasks before they were finished. Later, when she asked people what they remembered, they recalled the interrupted tasks about twice as often as the completed ones. This became known as the Zeigarnik effect.

One explanation is that an unfinished goal creates a kind of mental tension, which keeps the information active in memory. When the goal is completed, the tension is released. Now, I should mention that later studies haven't always found the same strong effect, so it's not a universal law. But it does have practical uses. For example, some students find that stopping a study session in the middle of a problem makes it easier to start again the next day.
